kf: **AGEP** is a pustular drug reaction: hundreds of tiny **non-follicular** sterile pustules on red, swollen skin, with fever.
Starts in the flexures and face **within hours to 2 days** of an antibiotic (aminopenicillins, macrolides) or other drug (hydroxychloroquine, diltiazem, terbinafine).
Neutrophilia is common; organ involvement is mild and uncommon.
Stop the drug, potent topical steroid and supportive care; settles in **1–2 weeks** with peeling.
Main differential: generalised pustular psoriasis (history of psoriasis, slower course).

sub: Rare (about 1–5 per million per year); any age; more women.

myths: **"Pustules mean infection"**: AGEP pustules are sterile; more antibiotics can make it worse.
patho_lead: Drug-specific T cells summon **neutrophils** into the top of the epidermis.

mech.t: Drug-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells migrate into the epidermis.
T cells and keratinocytes release **IL-8 (CXCL8)** and IL-17.
Neutrophils gather just under the stratum corneum, forming pinhead pustules.
mech.cap: AGEP: neutrophil-filled pustules collect just under the stratum corneum (subcorneal), not around hair follicles, over swollen inflamed skin.

mech.t: As pustules dry, the surface peels in collarettes over 1–2 weeks.

histo: Subcorneal or intraepidermal spongiform pustules, papillary oedema, eosinophils, sometimes necrotic keratinocytes.
comp: Superinfection; rarely liver, kidney or lung involvement; fluid loss in frail patients.
prog: Excellent once the drug is stopped; recurs on re-exposure.
